How to Choose Hiking Boots

The right hiking boots make a long day feel short, and the wrong pair can end a trip early. Before you look at brands or colors, think about where you hike, how much weight you carry and how often you go. A pair that is perfect for rocky alpine scrambles may feel stiff and heavy on a smooth forest path.

Pick the right cut

Low-cut hiking shoes are light and flexible, and they suit well-maintained trails and light loads. Mid-cut boots wrap the ankle, keep out small stones and give a little more support when the ground gets uneven. High-cut boots offer the most stability for heavy packs, loose scree and off-trail travel, but they take longer to break in and they weigh more on every step.

Decide on waterproofing

A waterproof membrane keeps your feet dry in puddles, wet grass and light snow. The trade-off is warmth: in hot, dry weather a waterproof boot can make your feet sweat, and once water gets in over the top it dries slowly. If you mostly hike in summer, a breathable mesh shoe that drains quickly can be the more comfortable choice.

Get the fit right

Shop late in the day, when your feet are at their largest, and bring the socks you plan to hike in. Your heel should stay put when you walk uphill, and your toes should not touch the front when you walk down a slope. Leave about a thumb's width of space in front of your longest toe. Walk around the store for at least ten minutes, and use an incline ramp if there is one.

Break them in

Wear new boots around the house, then on short walks, before you take them on a long hike. Most modern boots need only a few outings, but leather boots can take several weeks. Pay attention to hot spots and fix them early with different lacing or a better sock, rather than waiting for a blister on the trail.
